memoryText: But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Jonah 2:9 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
Jonah says these words from inside the great fish. He has just been swallowed, and he is saved. The last line has become one of the central statements of the Bible’s teaching on salvation.

“But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you.” Jonah contrasts himself with those who worship idols, mentioned in the previous verse. They give their loyalty to what is worthless. He will give thanks to the LORD. The sacrifice he promises is not an animal but the voice of thanksgiving. This echoes Psalm 50:14, which you read earlier: “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.”

“What I have vowed I will pay.” Jonah made vows in his distress. Many of us do the same: we promise God things in a crisis. Jonah says he will keep his word. It is a commitment to obedience, and one that he will be tested on when he is called again to go to Nineveh.

“Salvation belongs to the LORD!” This is the summary of the story and of the Bible. Salvation is not something we produce or earn. It is not found in idols, in human strength, or in our own efforts. It belongs to the LORD. He is the one who saves, from the storm, from the deep, from judgment, and from death.

The sailors were saved by recognizing it. Jonah was saved by his rescue. And Nineveh will be saved because the LORD is the God of salvation, whether the prophet likes it or not.

For the Christian, this is the heart of the gospel. “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). Say this verse when you are tempted to think that you saved yourself, or that someone is beyond saving.
weekInReview: This week you read the psalms of lament and justice: Psalms 74 and 77 on the fall of the sanctuary and the memory of the exodus, and Psalms 58, 82, 94, 109, 140, and 142 on the God who judges and defends the poor. You walked through the whole book of Hosea, from the unfaithful wife and the names of No Mercy and Not My People, through the lawsuit against Israel, to the cry of a heartbroken father, “How can I give you up?”, and the promise of healing in chapter 14. You also read the first half of Jonah: a prophet running away, a storm, pagan sailors who feared the LORD, and a fish appointed by God. The week taught that God’s love pursues the unfaithful, that he desires mercy and not sacrifice, and that salvation belongs to the LORD.
reflectionQuestions: Hosea shows God buying back an unfaithful wife. Where do you most need to remember that you were redeemed rather than earned your place?
Jesus said that the sign of Jonah points to his death and resurrection. How does Jonah’s rescue from the deep help you understand the gospel?
Jonah ran from a call that seemed too hard. Is there something you are running from that God is asking you to do?
prayerPrompts: Offer God thanksgiving for pursuing you.
Pray, “Salvation belongs to the LORD,” and mean it.
Thank Jesus, who entered the depths for you.
